explanation: A [[kw:frequency distribution]] organizes raw data into classes (intervals) and shows how many data points fall into each class.

Steps: 1. Determine the range (highest – lowest value). 2. Choose the number of classes (usually 5–20). 3. Compute class width (range ÷ number of classes, rounded up). 4. List class intervals and tally the data.
The [[kw:class frequency]] is the count in each class; the [[kw:relative frequency]] is the fraction or percent of total.
[[imp:Frequency distributions summarize large data sets and reveal patterns like central tendency, spread, and skewness.]]

formulaCard.title: Constructing a Frequency Distribution
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{Range} = \text{Max} - \text{Min}$$ $$\text{Class Width} = \frac{\text{Range}}{\text{Number of Classes}} \text{ (round up)}$$ $$\text{Relative Frequency} = \frac{\text{Class Frequency}}{\text{Total Observations}} \times 100$$
notes: Classes should not overlap and should cover all data.
Class boundaries must be clearly defined (e.g., 0‑9, 10‑19, etc.).

discoveryHook.scenario: A store records the number of customers each hour for 40 hours. Instead of a long list, the manager groups the data into intervals like 0‑9, 10‑19, etc., and counts how many hours fall into each interval. This [[kw:frequency distribution]] quickly shows the busiest times.

explanation: A [[kw:bar graph]] uses bars of equal width to represent the frequency or amount of each category.

Bars are separated by spaces to indicate distinct categories.
Bar graphs are ideal for comparing discrete categories (e.g., days of week, product types).

explanation: A [[kw:line graph]] plots data points (x, y) and connects them with lines to show trends over time or continuous data.
Time is usually on the x‑axis (horizontal); the variable measured on the y‑axis (vertical).
Line graphs highlight increases, decreases, and seasonal patterns.
Multiple lines can be plotted on the same graph to compare different series.
[[imp:Choose consistent intervals on the time axis to avoid distorting the trend.]]

formulaCard.title: Circle Graph Calculations
notes: The sum of all percentages must equal 100%.
The sum of slice angles must equal 360°.

explanation: A [[kw:circle graph]] (pie chart) represents data as slices of a circle, where each slice's angle is proportional to its percentage of the total.
Each category's percentage = (Category amount ÷ Total) × 100.
The angle of each slice = Percentage × 3.6° (since 100% = 360°).
Circle graphs are best for showing parts of a whole at a single point in time.
[[imp:Limit the number of slices to 5‑7 for clarity; too many slices make the chart hard to read.]]

visuals.title: Choosing the Right Graph

explanation: Apply the blueprint to data presentation problems:
1. Understand: identify the type of data (time series, categorical, part‑to‑whole) and the message to convey.

2. Solve: choose the appropriate graph (line for trends, bar for categories, circle for proportions). If computing a price relative, use $$\text{Price Relative} = \frac{\text{Current Price}}{\text{Base Price}} \times 100$$.
3. Conclude: create or interpret the graph; state the trend or comparison. Verify that axes are labeled, scales are appropriate, and the graph is not misleading.
This structured approach avoids using the wrong graph for the data.

formulaCard.title: Price Relative
notes: A price relative above 100 indicates an increase from the base period.

discoveryHook.scenario: A store manager wants to show monthly sales trends and also compare this month's prices to a base period. The blueprint helps decide which graph to use and how to calculate a [[kw:price relative]]: (Current price ÷ Base period price) × 100.
